title:
Interactive 3D
for websites
lead: The tools, how they work and when to use them
notes: 20 seconds. Today we will look at how interactive 3D reaches a website, where Blender, Three.js and WebGL fit, and how to choose a practical starting point. Total suggested presentation time: about 7 minutes.

title: What visitors can do
lead: The browser updates the scene as the visitor interacts.
rows: Rotate and zoom to see a product from different angles.
Change a finish, material or accessory.
Click a feature or follow a guided animation.
notes: 30 seconds. Imagine buying a camera online. You can inspect the lens, turn the camera around and select a feature to learn more. These actions make 3D useful. A fixed video is still a good choice when viewers only need to watch a story.

title: How the tools work together
lead: Each tool has a different job in the same workflow.
rows: Load the model and handle controls
Use the device’s GPU to draw it
notes: 45 seconds. Blender is the workshop, GLB is the delivery file, and Three.js organizes the live experience. WebGL or WebGPU connects browser rendering to the graphics processor. HTML and CSS provide the surrounding page. These technologies complement each other.

title: Blender: create the asset
lead: Best for 3D artists and motion designers preparing a detailed model.
rows: Create the shape, materials and animation.
Simplify heavy details and check scale and part names.
Export GLB and review it in the website viewer.
caption: Example product reference
notes: 45 seconds. A mesh describes the shape. A material describes how its surface reacts to light. Blender lets an artist author these and animate parts. The browser normally loads an exported asset, not the Blender project. Some complex materials or simulations need baking into simpler textures or animation. Accurate reference images and measurements improve the result.

title: Three.js: build the interaction
lead: Best for developers creating a custom 3D website experience.
rows: Load the model, place the camera and add lighting.
Add rotate, pan, zoom, hotspots or material changes.
Render the scene when it changes or while it animates.
notes: 45 seconds. Three.js is a JavaScript library. It supplies building blocks such as scenes, cameras, materials, loaders and controls. A developer combines them into a product viewer. It is useful when you need a specific look or behavior, but the team still builds loading states, accessibility and page integration.

title: WebGL and WebGPU: draw the pixels
lead: These browser APIs give rendering code access to the GPU.
rows: An established foundation for interactive browser graphics.
A newer API for rendering and GPU computation.
Use a supporting library or engine and test target devices.
notes: 40 seconds. The GPU is the processor that performs graphics work. These APIs receive geometry and rendering instructions and produce the canvas image. Most product teams use them through a library rather than writing the entire renderer. WebGPU is not automatically faster and support varies. Three.js has a WebGPU renderer with a WebGL 2 fallback, subject to feature compatibility.

title: Other tools worth knowing
lead: Choose a starting point based on the project and the team.
rows: Add a web component and GLB
Integrate or host the engine app
notes: 55 seconds. These are recommendations, not a universal ranking. model-viewer provides a focused product-viewing component. Spline supports visual scene design and embeds. React Three Fiber expresses Three.js scenes as React components and still requires 3D knowledge. Babylon.js and PlayCanvas are useful for richer applications. Check the requirements, current export options and mobile behavior before choosing.

title: Getting 3D onto a website
lead: The same basic workflow applies to Webflow and custom websites.
rows: Create and approve a lightweight GLB asset.
Choose an embedded viewer or a custom Three.js scene.
Host the viewer and assets, then add them to the page.
Check loading, touch controls and the published URL.
notes: 45 seconds. A web component sits directly in the page. An iframe embeds a separately hosted viewer and is often convenient for a website builder. A direct JavaScript integration gives more control over page behavior. Use public HTTPS asset URLs for publishing. localhost is only a preview on your own computer.

title: Who does what
lead: A shared handoff connects the visual idea to the working website.
rows: Defines layout, controls and the first view.
Specifies timing, transitions and interruption behavior.
Delivers the model, materials and animation clips.
Builds interaction, loading states and deployment.
notes: 35 seconds. Agree on the initial camera angle and interaction before building the whole scene. Artists provide named parts and approved exports. Motion designers explain what happens when a visitor interrupts a transition. Developers test the resulting experience. Review the asset together inside the real browser.

title: What makes the result good
lead: Visual quality and usability need attention together.
rows: Match the product’s shape before adding visual effects.
Optimize assets and measure on real phones.
Provide clear controls, reduced motion and a static fallback.
notes: 40 seconds. Lighting cannot fix inaccurate geometry. Reduce expensive geometry, textures and effects based on measured performance rather than an arbitrary polygon limit. Keep product information in HTML, offer a reset view, preserve normal page scrolling and provide a useful image if 3D fails to load.

title: A simple starting point
lead: One model and one useful interaction are enough for a first version.
rows: Try Spline, then test the published result.
notes: 30 seconds. The main takeaway: Blender creates the asset, a viewer or engine manages the experience, and a browser graphics API draws it. Choose the simplest approach that supports the visitor’s task. These recommendations are based on the documented capabilities, not performance benchmarks. Sources throughout the deck are in the speaker notes.
